task.display: Choose File → Save As, or press `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `S`, then confirm the filename.

summary.display: In real Blender, save desk-tray-01-start.blend. Save often.

description.display: You completed this tutorial. Orbit, pan, and zoom the live model here, then download the checkpoint and continue in real Blender. Save a new version before experimenting.

task.display: Download a checkpoint, or return to the course.

summary.display: Save your real Blender project before leaving.

description.display: Scene units belong to the scene. Find the Properties editor at the right, then its Scene tab: the icon combines a cone, sphere, and light. This is different from the Item Sidebar inside the viewport.

task.display: Click the Scene Properties tab.

summary.display: You selected Scene Properties. Next, open its Units section.

description.display: The Units section is collapsed. We start without a unit system so you can configure it yourself. These scene settings travel with your Blender file.

task.display: Click the Units heading to expand it.

summary.display: Unit System currently reads None. The scale and length controls become useful after choosing Metric.

description.display: Metric enables familiar physical measurements. Choosing Millimeters later changes the displayed length unit; Unit Scale controls how Blender units relate to physical size.

task.display: Open Unit System and choose Metric.

summary.display: Metric is selected. The scale is still 1, so one Blender unit currently represents one meter.

description.display: For this course, use Unit Scale 0.001: one Blender unit represents one millimeter. This is a course convention, not the only valid printing workflow. Changing Unit Scale changes the interpretation of existing geometry, so set it before modeling.

task.display: Double-click Unit Scale, type `0` `.` `0` `0` `1`, then press `Enter`.

summary.display: Unit Scale is 0.001. A default two-unit cube now represents 2 millimeters on each side.

description.display: Length controls how distances are displayed. Set it to Millimeters so dimensions and viewport clipping distances use the same unit as the tray project.

task.display: Open Length and choose Millimeters.

summary.display: Distances are displayed in millimeters. This does not resize the mesh.

description.display: Viewport settings are separate from scene settings. Open the Sidebar inside the 3D Viewport. You can use the View menu or the N shortcut learned in Meet Blender.

task.display: Choose View → Sidebar, or focus the viewport and press `N`.

summary.display: The Sidebar is open. Its Item tab shows the cube dimensions; the View tab contains clipping settings.

description.display: The Sidebar has vertical tabs on its right edge. Choose View to find the viewport lens and clipping distances. Leave Focal Length at 50 millimeters for this course.

task.display: Click the Sidebar’s View tab.

summary.display: Clip Start and End define the nearest and farthest surfaces the viewport can display. They do not cut or resize your model.

description.display: Clip Start hides surfaces closer to the viewpoint than this distance. If a close-up seems sliced open, reduce this value. Use 0.1 millimeters for this course, and reduce it further only when the detail needs it.

task.display: Double-click Clip Start, enter `0` `.` `1`, then press `Enter`.

summary.display: The near clipping distance is 0.1 millimeters. This is a viewport setting; a render camera has separate clipping controls.

description.display: End hides surfaces beyond the far clipping distance. Use 10000 millimeters, or 10 meters, for this course workspace. Avoid making the range unnecessarily enormous: an extreme range can reduce depth precision.

task.display: Double-click End, enter `1` `0` `0` `0` `0`, then press `Enter`.

summary.display: The viewport range is now 0.1 to 10000 millimeters. These settings affect this 3D Viewport, not every editor in every Blender file.

description.display: A startup file stores the current scene and workspace, including scene units and this viewport’s settings. Save it before building the tray, so future new files do not start with your finished model. Our practice scene still contains the default Cube, Camera, and Light.

task.display: Choose File → Defaults → Save Startup File.

summary.display: Blender asks before replacing the startup file. Saving a startup file is different from saving a named project with Save As.

description.display: In real Blender, this replaces your previous startup scene. In this simulation, only the practice checkpoint changes. If you want to keep a customized startup in real Blender, save a separate scene template instead.

task.display: Click Overwrite to save this simulated startup configuration.

summary.display: Your setup is saved. In real Blender, test File → New → General after saving any current work. Check Metric, 0.001, Millimeters, and the View tab’s clipping values.

description.display: You configured scene units, viewport clipping, and a startup file. The downloadable setup scene is an optional recovery point. Open a new file in real Blender and verify the settings, then continue to the tray lessons.

task.display: Keep Blender open and save each project under its own name.

summary.display: Always check the exported model’s dimensions in your slicer. A startup file does not control every exporter’s scale.

description.display: The selected object receives your changes. Click the cube itself, rather than empty space.

task.display: Click the cube in the viewport.

summary.display: The orange outline identifies the active object.

description.display: G starts Move. Move the pointer to judge the result visually. Hold Shift while moving for one-tenth-speed precision, then release Shift to return to normal speed. Left-click or Enter confirms; Escape cancels. This is a practice copy; the next exercise starts from a fresh cube.

task.display: Press `G`, move the pointer, then hold `Shift` and move again. Left-click or press `Enter` to confirm.

summary.display: You practiced visual transformation and Shift precision. The next checkpoint restores the cube for a new exercise.

description.display: R starts Rotate. Move the pointer to judge the result visually. Hold Shift while moving for one-tenth-speed precision, then release Shift to return to normal speed. Left-click or Enter confirms; Escape cancels. This is a practice copy; the next exercise starts from a fresh cube.

task.display: Press `R`, move the pointer, then hold `Shift` and move again. Left-click or press `Enter` to confirm.

summary.display: You practiced visual transformation and Shift precision. The next checkpoint restores the cube for a new exercise.

description.display: S starts Scale. Move the pointer to judge the result visually. Hold Shift while moving for one-tenth-speed precision, then release Shift to return to normal speed. Left-click or Enter confirms; Escape cancels. This is a practice copy; the next exercise starts from a fresh cube.

task.display: Press `S`, move the pointer, then hold `Shift` and move again. Left-click or press `Enter` to confirm.

summary.display: You practiced visual transformation and Shift precision. The next checkpoint restores the cube for a new exercise.

description.display: G starts Blender’s Move operation. X constrains it to the X axis. Numeric entry sets the distance, and Enter confirms. Escape or right-click cancels the operation. The mesh previews while you move the pointer and while you type. The numeric entry record near the top of the viewport shows your input before you confirm.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press `G` → `X` → `1` → `Enter`. Watch the preview before Enter.

summary.display: The object moved 1 mm along X. The view and object dimensions stayed unchanged.

description.display: An absolute Location value describes where the origin is, not how far to move.

task.display: Double-click Location X to 0 mm, then press Enter.

summary.display: The object returned to X = 0.

description.display: Z is vertical. Rotation around Z turns the object in the horizontal plane. The mesh previews while you move the pointer and while you type. The numeric entry record near the top of the viewport shows your input before you confirm.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press `R` → `Z` → `4` → `5` → `Enter`. Watch the preview before Enter.

summary.display: The mesh changed orientation; the view stayed fixed.

description.display: We want axis-aligned dimensions while building the tray.

task.display: Double-click Rotation Z to 0, then press Enter.

summary.display: The cube is aligned with X and Y again.

description.display: This checkpoint pulls the view back to leave room for a 100 × 70 × 18 mm tray. Dimensions changes the size of the selected object in Object Mode.

task.display: Double-click Dimensions X to 100 mm, then press Enter.

summary.display: X is now 100 mm. The other dimensions have not changed.

description.display: Independent dimensions let us turn the cube into a rectangular blank.

task.display: Double-click Dimensions Y to 70 mm, then press Enter.

summary.display: The footprint is now 100 × 70 mm.

description.display: The outside height is 18 mm. The cavity will be cut into this volume in Edit Mode.

task.display: Double-click Dimensions Z to 18 mm, then press Enter.

summary.display: The tray blank now measures 100 × 70 × 18 mm.

description.display: Changing dimensions in Object Mode changes scale. Apply Scale preserves the visible size while making the scale values 1. This gives dimension-sensitive mesh tools a consistent starting point.

task.display: Choose Object → Apply → Scale. Use the menu here; you will practice Ctrl+A next.

summary.display: The blank keeps its dimensions. Scale is now 1 on every axis.

description.display: The same starting checkpoint is restored so you can practice the keyboard route. Changing dimensions in Object Mode changes scale. Apply Scale preserves the visible size while making the scale values 1. This gives dimension-sensitive mesh tools a consistent starting point.

task.display: Focus the viewport and press `Ctrl` + `A` and choose Scale.

summary.display: The blank keeps its dimensions. Scale is now 1 on every axis.

description.display: The cube origin is at its center. With an 18 mm height, the center must be at Z = 9 mm for the bottom to sit at Z = 0.

task.display: Double-click Location Z to 9 mm, then press Enter.

summary.display: The bottom is now at zero. The next checkpoint preserves the blank as actual Blender geometry.

description.display: Before editing topology, save a separate checkpoint. You can return to it if an experiment goes wrong. In real Blender, Ctrl+S saves the current named file; Ctrl+Shift+S creates a separately named version.

task.display: Choose File → Save As, or press `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `S`, then confirm the filename.

summary.display: In real Blender, save desk-tray-02-sized.blend. The Blank download below is available if you need to catch up.

description.display: You completed this tutorial. Orbit, pan, and zoom the live model here, then download the checkpoint and continue in real Blender. Save a new version before experimenting.

task.display: Download a checkpoint, or return to the course.

summary.display: Save your real Blender project before leaving.

description.display: Object Mode transforms the whole object. Edit Mode changes its vertices, edges, and faces. The Layout workspace can contain either mode.

task.display: Open the mode selector and choose Edit Mode. Use the menu here; you will practice Tab next.

summary.display: You are now working on the mesh inside the object.

quiz.display: Is Edit Mode a separate workspace?

description.display: The same starting checkpoint is restored so you can practice the keyboard route. Object Mode transforms the whole object. Edit Mode changes its vertices, edges, and faces. The Layout workspace can contain either mode.

task.display: Focus the viewport and press `Tab`, then finish the same action.

summary.display: You are now working on the mesh inside the object.

description.display: Vertex Select is already active: the first of the three selection icons in the header is highlighted. This mode lets you select the mesh’s corner points. A plain click selects one vertex; Shift-click adds another or removes it from the selection.

task.display: Click one visible corner vertex. Then hold `Shift` and click a different corner to add it.

summary.display: You selected one vertex, then added another with Shift-click. Edge Select and Face Select, beside Vertex Select in the header, let you select different parts of the same mesh.

description.display: Edges are the lines connecting pairs of vertices. The middle selection icon switches to Edge Select so you can select those lines. For this step, just change the selection mode.

task.display: Click Edge Select. Or press `2` on the top row of your keyboard.

summary.display: Edge Select is active. The third icon beside it switches to Face Select.

description.display: Faces are the surfaces bounded by edges. Our tray begins by editing its top face.

task.display: Click Face Select. Or press `3` on the top row of your keyboard.

summary.display: Top-row 3 chooses Face Select. Numpad keys control views instead.

description.display: Select only the broad top surface. The inset will operate on this selection. The orange fill shows the chosen face.

task.display: Click the broad top face of the blank.

summary.display: The selected top face is ready for the wall inset.

description.display: Inset Faces creates a smaller face surrounded by a rim. The rim becomes our wall footprint. The mesh previews while you move the pointer and while you type. The numeric entry record near the top of the viewport shows your input before you confirm.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press `I` → `3` → `Enter`. Watch the preview before Enter.

summary.display: The inner face measures 94 × 64 mm. The surrounding rim is 3 mm wide.

description.display: Extrusion creates geometry and then moves it. Escape cancels the movement, leaving the new geometry at zero distance. Ctrl+Z removes that extrusion. This is different from simply cancelling Move or Rotate.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press E, then Escape, then Ctrl+Z.

summary.display: The extrusion geometry was undone. You are back at the inset checkpoint, ready to make the cavity.

description.display: Extrude the selected inner face downward by 15 mm. Starting from a height of 18 mm leaves a 3 mm floor. Enter a negative value to move down Z. The mesh previews while you move the pointer and while you type. The numeric entry record near the top of the viewport shows your input before you confirm.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press `E` → `-` → `1` → `5` → `Enter`. Watch the preview before Enter.

summary.display: The tray has an open cavity, 3 mm walls, and a 3 mm floor.

description.display: This is a useful recovery point. Save a version before adding bevel geometry. In real Blender, Ctrl+S saves the current named file; Ctrl+Shift+S creates a separately named version.

task.display: Choose File → Save As, or press `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `S`, then confirm the filename.

summary.display: In real Blender, save desk-tray-03-cavity.blend, then experiment on a copy.

description.display: Edge Select is active and no edges are selected. We will bevel only the four outside edges around the top rim. A plain click selects one edge; Shift-click adds or removes another edge.

task.display: Click one outside top rim edge. Hold `Shift` and click the other three outside top edges.

summary.display: All four outside top rim edges are selected. The inner opening, vertical edges, and bottom edges remain unselected.

description.display: Bevel the four outer rim edges you selected. A 0.6 mm bevel with three segments and Profile 0.5 creates a rounded transition with real geometry. Move the pointer to preview the width, or type a number. Scroll the wheel during the operation to change the number of segments. You can zoom in before starting to inspect the edge shape.

task.display: Click the viewport. Press `Ctrl` + `B`, type `0` `.` `6`, scroll up twice for 3 segments, then `Enter`.

summary.display: The outer rim now contains three curved segments across its 0.6 mm bevel. The cavity and floor remain intact. Orbit and zoom to inspect the new geometry in real Blender.

description.display: This inspection checkpoint starts with the finished mesh deselected. Face Orientation reveals reversed faces. Find the option in Viewport Overlays, under Geometry, then inspect all sides in real Blender.

task.display: Open the Viewport Overlays arrow, enable Face Orientation under Geometry, then click the viewport to close the popover.

summary.display: Our generated mesh has no boundary or non-manifold edges. That does not replace checking dimensions, thickness, and sliced layers.

description.display: Return to Object Mode before exporting the selected tray. Keep the editable Blender project as your source.

task.display: Choose Object Mode in the mode selector, or press `Tab` in the viewport.

summary.display: The entire tray is selected for saving and export.

description.display: STL stores a mesh, not the complete Blender project. Save your .blend first so you can revise the design later. In real Blender, Ctrl+S saves the current named file; Ctrl+Shift+S creates a separately named version.

task.display: Choose File → Save As, or press `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `S`, then confirm the filename.

summary.display: In real Blender, save desk-tray-04-finished.blend.

description.display: Our checkpoint stores coordinates in millimeters. Export selected objects with Scale 1 and Scene Unit off. The generated STL has been reimported and checked at 100 × 70 × 18 mm.

task.display: Choose File → Export → STL (.stl), then Export STL.

summary.display: The tray is exported as desk-tray.stl. Next, open the simulated Bambu Studio workspace and import this model to verify its dimensions and orientation.

quiz.display: What must you check after importing into the slicer?

description.display: The Blender model is ready to check in a slicer. Use the course’s launch button to open simulated Bambu Studio, then choose Prepare. In real life, launch Bambu Studio from your desktop or Start menu.

task.display: Click Open Bambu Studio, then select Prepare.

summary.display: Bambu Studio is open in Prepare with an empty build plate.

description.display: Use Add model to import the STL you exported. This practice file is the actual Blender-generated tray, including its rounded bevel. Importing places the mesh on the plate without slicing it.

task.display: Click Add model, select desk-tray.stl, then choose Open.

summary.display: Your tray is on the Bambu Studio build plate, with its flat bottom down and cavity facing up.

description.display: Select the tray and read its size in Bambu Studio. It should measure 100 × 70 × 18 mm. Check that the open cavity faces up and the flat bottom rests on the plate. If dimensions differ in real life, review your Blender export scale before slicing.

task.display: Click the tray on the plate to select it and show its dimensions.

summary.display: The imported STL measures 100 × 70 × 18 mm. Continue to the Bambu Studio slicing course to choose the correct printer and material, slice the model, and inspect the layers before printing.

description.display: You modeled a tray, selected and beveled its rim, exported it, and imported the actual STL into Bambu Studio. Inspect it here with orbit, pan, and zoom, then continue with the slicer lessons.

task.display: Inspect the tray, then continue to the Bambu Studio slicing course.

summary.display: Save often. Keep the editable Blender file alongside your STL and Bambu Studio project.
